dimensions.note: Reviewed for the new b2-key kind. The secret is an `<applicationKeyId>:<applicationKey>` pair, marked sensitive by the shared CredentialInputSchema, and reaches only btoa() for the Basic header -- it is never placed in a URL, a detail string, or a resource attribute. `subject` is an IDENTIFIER: parseB2Subject REJECTS any value containing ':', so a pasted key pair cannot be stored where an id belongs, mirroring parsePveSubject's rejection of '='. The `on behalf of ${target}` detail interpolates only a validated applicationKeyId. Confirmed no code path logs the secret.

The probe emits no logs of its own; every outcome travels as a structured ProbeResult, consistent with the other four kinds. Failure details name the HTTP status or the missing contract field, which is enough to diagnose without echoing request or response bodies.

Every remote interaction is guarded: fetch rejection, non-2xx on both calls, non-JSON on both bodies, an authorize 200 missing apiUrl/authorizationToken/accountId, an absent key row, and a non-numeric expirationTimestamp. The load-bearing decision is that an unreadable expiry reports `unreachable` and NEVER `noExpiry` -- those look identical in a summary and mean opposite things. GAP FOUND AND CLOSED: six of these branches had no direct test at review time; added in PR #7, which changes no production code and leaves this cacheHash byte-identical.

9 tests shipped with the kind, covering the three named traps (ms-vs-seconds, 401-means-two-things, expired-keys-are-deleted), subject routing, malformed-secret short-circuit, and baseUrl trailing-slash handling. The adversarial pass found the failure paths under-covered relative to the sibling pve-token probe; PR #7 adds 6 more, bringing the suite to 60 passing. Also verified end-to-end against LIVE Backblaze rather than stubs alone: status ok, 89 days remaining on a key minted with a 90-day duration -- the arithmetic check that would have caught the units bug independently of the unit test.

Read-only by construction: two GETs, and no method that can create, rotate or revoke. Re-running is free and produces no side effects, which is what makes the daily unattended schedule safe against production credentials. Both requests carry the shared timeoutMs via AbortSignal.timeout, so a hung endpoint cannot stall the audit.

B2 native API v3: GET b2_authorize_account with HTTP Basic, then GET b2_list_keys with accountId/maxKeyCount/startApplicationKeyId. The storage apiUrl is DISCOVERED from the authorize response rather than configured, which is correct -- it is per-account and B2 does not document it as stable. startApplicationKeyId begins the listing AT the target so maxKeyCount=1 returns exactly the row of interest; the returned applicationKeyId is re-checked because B2 returns the NEXT key when the target is gone. Contract confirmed against the live API, not only against stubs.

No handles, no temp files, no caches. Response bodies are consumed by .json() on every path that reads them; paths that ignore the body return before reading it, which Deno does not require explicit disposal for.

Adds exactly parseB2Secret and parseB2Subject to the exported surface, matching the existing parsePveToken/parsePveSubject precedent -- exported so the parsing rules can be asserted directly rather than only through a probe. probeB2Key itself stays module-private and is reached through probeFor, like every other kind. The archive publishes only credential_expiry.ts, README.md and LICENSE.md; the test file is not shipped.

b2BaseUrl is z.string().url() with a real default (https://api.backblazeb2.com). That deliberately differs from pveBaseUrl's unroutable placeholder, and the reason is recorded inline: B2's authorization host is universal, so a real default cannot silently probe someone else's estate the way a real PVE default could. The kind is added to the PROBE_KINDS enum, so an unknown kind is rejected at parse time rather than at run time.

Not applicable in the usual sense -- the probe creates no resources. Worth recording that B2 DELETES an expired application key rather than retaining it as expired, so this credential's lifetime ends by disappearing; that is handled explicitly as authFailed rather than being allowed to read as noExpiry.

Read-only by design and by intent: this model has no method that can create, rotate or revoke, which is what makes it safe to schedule unattended. A b2-key probe deliberately does not gain one -- the provisioner key it reads holds writeKeys, so adding a write path here would turn a monitor into a mint.

Two preflights, both ordered before any network call or any decision. parseB2Secret short-circuits a malformed secret with no request made (asserted by test). The listKeys capability is read from the authorize response rather than inferred from a 401 -- necessary because B2 answers 401 both for a refused key and for a valid key lacking capability, and those are an outage versus a monitoring gap.

Unchanged by this kind. The resource instance name still derives from the credential `id`, so the b2-key entry resolves onto its keyring/credentials.yaml row exactly as the other four do -- the mapping contract restored in swamp-homelab#74.
Writes the same credential/audit resource shape as every other kind; no new fields and no schema change, so existing queries and the notifyToday alert gating are unaffected.

Purely additive: one new enum member and one new globalArg with a default. Existing model configs parse and behave identically, and no stored data changes shape. The exhaustiveness `never` in probeFor is what guarantees the enum and the implementations cannot drift apart -- adding a kind without a probe fails the type-check rather than falling through to another kind's rules.
